nurse.intro: Learn the practice of nursing — from vital signs and medication to patient communication and clinical records. Master the daily skills that keep patients safe in hospitals, clinics, and community settings.

skillDomains.name: Clinical Care
skillDomains.description: Direct patient care — assessment, hygiene, wound care, and monitoring.

skills.name: Vital Signs
skills.description: Measure and interpret the five core vitals that tell you what's happening inside a patient.

modules.title: The five vitals
modules.content:
Vital signs are the fastest way to know if a patient is stable, deteriorating, or improving. There are five:

  1. Temperature — normal 36.1–37.2°C
  2. Pulse — normal 60–100 beats/min at rest
  3. Respiratory rate — normal 12–20 breaths/min
  4. Blood pressure — normal 90/60 to 120/80 mmHg
  5. Oxygen saturation (SpO₂) — normal 95–100%

Recorded together, they tell a story. Recorded individually, they tell you nothing.

modules.title: Taking vitals correctly
modules.content:
Pulse

Place two fingers (never thumb) on the radial artery at the wrist. Count for 30 seconds and multiply by 2. Note rhythm and strength, not just rate.

Blood pressure

Patient seated, arm supported at heart level. Cuff size must match arm size — a too-small cuff reads high.

Respiratory rate

Count without telling the patient — breathing changes when people are aware they're being watched.

Temperature

Clean the thermometer between patients. Never use an oral thermometer on a patient who has eaten or drunk in the last 15 minutes.

steps.q: Temp 38.5°C, pulse 110, RR 24. What's the picture?
o: Fever with tachycardia and tachypnoea — infection likely
steps.f: All three elevated together suggests systemic infection. Report to the doctor.

steps.q: BP 88/55, pulse 120, patient dizzy when standing. What's happening?
o: Hypotension — possible dehydration, bleeding, or sepsis
steps.f: Low BP with high pulse is a red flag for shock. Act immediately.

steps.q: SpO₂ 89% on room air. What do you do?
o: Ask the patient to breathe deeper
steps.f: SpO₂ below 92% needs oxygen and immediate escalation. Do not wait.

modules.title: Recognise a deteriorating patient
modules.prompt: You're on a ward. A patient who was stable 2 hours ago now has: Temp 39.2°C, pulse 118, RR 26, BP 100/65, SpO₂ 93%. Describe what you do, in order.
modules.context: Early recognition of deterioration saves lives. Nurses are often the first to see the change.
rubric: Recognises this as a deterioration (multiple vitals abnormal)
Repeats the vitals to confirm
Notifies the doctor or senior nurse immediately
Applies oxygen if available and indicated
Checks for other signs (urine output, mental state, skin colour)
Documents the vitals, time, and escalation
Stays with the patient until help arrives

modules.title: Build a vitals tracking chart
modules.prompt: Design a chart for tracking vitals over 24 hours for a single patient. It must make deterioration obvious at a glance.
steps: Include rows for each vital sign
Include columns for each time checked
Add a section for escalation notes
Make it simple enough to fill in during a busy shift

skills.name: Infection Control
skills.description: Stop the spread. Hand hygiene, PPE, and sterile technique save more lives than any drug.

modules.title: The five moments of hand hygiene
modules.content:
WHO's five moments for hand hygiene:

  1. Before touching a patient
  2. Before a clean/aseptic procedure
  3. After body fluid exposure risk
  4. After touching a patient
  5. After touching patient surroundings

How to wash

Soap and water for 40–60 seconds. Alcohol rub for 20–30 seconds. Cover every surface: palms, backs, between fingers, thumbs, fingertips, wrists.

Skipping hand hygiene is the single biggest cause of hospital-acquired infection. There is no excuse.

modules.title: When to wash, when to rub

steps.q: You're about to insert a catheter. Hand hygiene?
steps.f: Aseptic procedures require soap and water — alcohol rub doesn't kill all organisms, especially C. difficile spores.

steps.q: Hands are visibly soiled. What do you use?
steps.f: Visibly soiled hands always require soap and water. Alcohol rub is for clean hands.

steps.q: You've just removed gloves after examining a patient. Do you need hand hygiene?
steps.f: Gloves are not perfect barriers. Always wash hands after removal.

modules.title: PPE — when and how
modules.content:
Gloves

For every contact with body fluids. Not for routine patient contact.

Aprons and gowns

When clothing may be contaminated. Change between patients.

Masks

Surgical mask for droplet precautions. N95/respirator for airborne (TB, measles, COVID).

Eye protection

Any procedure with splash risk.

Order of putting on (donning)

Gown → Mask → Goggles → Gloves.

Order of taking off (doffing)

Gloves → Goggles → Gown → Mask. Hand hygiene after each step.

modules.title: Care for a TB patient
modules.prompt: You're assigned to care for a patient with active pulmonary tuberculosis in a general ward. Describe the PPE you wear, the precautions you take, and how you protect other patients.
modules.context: TB is airborne. Standard surgical masks are not enough.
rubric: Wears an N95 or FFP2 respirator, not a surgical mask
Ensures the patient is in a negative-pressure room or well-ventilated single room
Patient wears a surgical mask when moving through the ward
Keeps the door closed
Limits the number of staff entering
Uses airborne precautions signage
Ensures visitors are screened

skillDomains.name: Medication
skillDomains.description: Give the right drug, to the right patient, at the right dose, at the right time.

skills.name: Medication Administration
skills.description: The five rights and how to get them right every time.

modules.title: The five rights
modules.content:
Every medication administration checks five things:

  1. Right patient — confirm ID
  2. Right drug — read the label twice
  3. Right dose — calculate, don't guess
  4. Right route — oral, IV, IM, SC, topical
  5. Right time — within the prescribed window

Medication errors kill. Every step has a reason. Skip one and you may kill a patient.

steps.q: A patient's chart says Amoxicillin 500mg TID. You have 250mg capsules. How many per dose?
An unconscious patient is prescribed oral tablets. What do you do?
o: Check for an alternative route with the prescriber
steps.f: Never give oral meds to an unconscious patient — aspiration risk. Call the prescriber.

steps.q: You've prepared a dose but the patient is in the bathroom. What do you do?
o: Leave the dose at the bedside
Wait, or return later with the dose still in hand
Give it to the next patient
steps.f: Never leave medication unattended. Never give to the wrong patient. Return with the dose when the patient is available.

modules.title: Respond to a medication error
modules.prompt: You realise you've just given a patient 10mg of a drug instead of the prescribed 1mg. Walk through exactly what you do, in order.
modules.context: Errors happen. What matters is what you do next. Honesty and speed save lives.
rubric: Assess the patient immediately for adverse effects
Call the doctor or prescriber without delay
Tell the patient and family what happened
Monitor the patient closely for several hours
Document the error factually in the notes and incident system
Do NOT try to hide it or adjust the record
Participate in a review to prevent recurrence

modules.title: Design a medication administration record
modules.prompt: Create a template for recording medication administration on a ward. It must be clear, unambiguous, and easy to audit.
steps: Columns for drug name, dose, route, time
Space for the administering nurse's initials
Space for any omitted doses and the reason
A space for allergies at the top

skillDomains.name: Patient Communication
skillDomains.description: Listen, explain, and support. Communication is a clinical skill.

skills.name: Therapeutic Communication
skills.description: Talk to patients in a way that builds trust and reduces fear.

modules.title: Communication is treatment
modules.content:
Patients remember two things from a hospital stay: whether they were treated kindly, and whether they understood what was happening to them.

The basics

  • Greet the patient by name
  • Sit down if you can — sitting says "I have time for you"
  • Make eye contact
  • Use plain language, not medical jargon
  • Ask open questions: "How are you feeling today?" not "Any pain?"
  • Let silence happen — patients often say the most important thing after a pause

steps.q: How would you say "hypertension" to a patient with low literacy?
steps.f: Simple, common words. Patients can understand "high blood pressure".

steps.q: A patient is frightened about an upcoming operation. Best response?
steps.f: Open the conversation. Fear lives in specifics, and so does reassurance.

steps.q: A patient starts crying. What do you do?
o: Offer a tissue, sit quietly, let them cry
steps.f: Silent presence is powerful. Don't rush past emotion.

modules.title: Communicate a difficult diagnosis
modules.prompt: A patient's test results show they have a serious, life-limiting illness. The doctor has asked you to prepare the patient for the news. Describe how you would approach this conversation.
modules.context: The way news is delivered affects how the patient copes for the rest of their life.
modules.placeholder:
Preparing the patient:
If they ask me directly:
After the doctor speaks:
rubric: Ensures privacy and enough time
Asks the patient what they already know
Checks whether they want family present
Does not give the diagnosis if it's the doctor's role — prepares but doesn't preempt
Uses clear, gentle language
Allows silence and emotion
Offers support and a follow-up plan

skillDomains.name: Clinical Records
skillDomains.description: Document everything. If it isn't written, it didn't happen.

skills.name: Documentation
skills.description: Write clear, accurate, timely clinical notes.

modules.title: Why records matter
modules.content:
Clinical records serve three purposes:

  1. Patient care — other clinicians read your notes to continue care
  2. Legal protection — notes are evidence if something goes wrong
  3. Audit and improvement — patterns of problems become visible in the data

Rules

  • Write at the time of care, not hours later
  • Use black ink or the electronic record
  • Never erase — draw a single line through errors and initial them
  • Never write for someone else
  • Use objective language: "Patient reports pain" not "Patient is exaggerating"

steps.q: A patient complains of pain. Best note?
o: Patient says pain is 7/10, sharp, in lower right abdomen
steps.f: Be specific: location, quality, severity. That's clinically useful.

steps.q: You gave paracetamol at 14:00. What must the note include?
o: Drug, dose, route, time, and effect
steps.f: Full details: paracetamol 1g orally at 14:00. Plus effect noted later.

steps.q: You made an error in the previous entry. What do you do?
o: Draw a single line through it, initial, and write the correction with date/time
steps.f: Single line through, initial and date. Never erase. Never leave ambiguity about what was corrected.
